clue.text: Tramp in hospital — old boy needs oxygen

parts.note: H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital
OB is the standard abbreviation for an old boy, a former pupil
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A down-and-out lies in a hospital bed while an elderly man gasps for oxygen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in hospital' looks like where the tramp is, but it simply supplies the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobo is an American word for a homeless wanderer, a synonym of tramp.

clue.text: With gardening aid, weed round end of beds and whistle

indicators.note: going round something means wrapping around it, so one word encloses the other
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that last letter is used here

parts.note: to hoe is to weed with a garden tool
the final letter of beds
to pipe is to whistle or play a high note

explanation.surface: A gardener tidies the flower beds, whistling while they weed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' only links; 'round' puts the single letter from beds inside the weeding word.
explanation.definitionFit: A hosepipe is a flexible tube used for watering plants, a common piece of garden equipment.

clue.text: Boy hasn't finished a long fried sausage

indicators.note: something not finished is missing its ending, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: taken as written, before trimming

indicators.note: frying scrambles and cooks things up, signalling the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lad who has not finished eating a long fried sausage at breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fried' reads as cooking the sausage, but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bologna is a large smoked sausage named after the Italian city, the origin of baloney.

clue.text: Drunk by male wearing very large garment

indicators.note: by means beside, so one piece is placed next to the other
a word wearing another has it on, so it is enclosed by the outer word

parts.note: huge is a synonym of very large
M is the abbreviation for male
tight is informal for drunk

explanation.surface: A man the worse for drink sports an enormous item of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: A hug-me-tight is a short, close-fitting knitted jacket or shawl, an old-fashioned word many solvers will not know.
explanation.definitionFit: A hug-me-tight is a snug woollen wrap or bolero, so it is an item of clothing.

clue.text: Join group on top of Everest

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: a unit is a group, such as a military unit

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of Everest

explanation.surface: An invitation to join a climbing team at the summit of Everest.
explanation.definitionFit: To unite is to join together into one, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Essay from Dr No, with diagram

parts.note: MO is a Medical Officer, a doctor
taken as written
a graph is a kind of diagram; with just joins it on

explanation.surface: An essay on the Bond film Dr No, illustrated with a diagram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dr No' reads as the Bond villain, but the two words split: Dr is a doctor, MO, and No stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: A monograph is a detailed scholarly treatise on a single subject, a kind of essay.

clue.text: Amphibian that's burrowed down for food?

parts.note: a toad is an amphibian
something burrowed down is in the hole

explanation.surface: A frog-like creature digs itself into the ground in search of something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the 'food' is not what a toad eats but a dish: toad-in-the-hole is a British meal of sausages baked in batter.
explanation.definitionFit: Toad-in-the-hole is a traditional British dish of sausages cooked in Yorkshire pudding batter.

clue.text: Idle talk about it, King Edward's spats

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the others

parts.note: gas is informal for idle chatter
taken as written
ER stands for Edwardus Rex, King Edward's royal cipher

explanation.surface: Gossip about a king's quarrels, as if King Edward were having spats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spats' looks like quarrels, but it means ankle coverings worn over shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Spats are short cloth coverings for the ankle and shoe, which are a kind of gaiter.

clue.text: 'Game in mist spoiled' — that's a self-evident statement

indicators.note: something spoiled is ruined and messed up, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: RU is rugby union, the game
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rugby match ruined by fog is, obviously, a statement of the obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: RU goes into MIST, and the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A truism is a statement so obviously true it hardly needs saying.

clue.text: Choice made by son voting

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
an election is a vote

explanation.surface: A young man casts his first ballot and makes his choice.
explanation.definitionFit: A selection is a choice, the act of picking from options.

clue.text: Weathy clientele in freight business

definitions.meaning: first meaning: rich customers, originally those who arrived by private coach
second meaning, literally: the trade of conveying goods

explanation.surface: Rich customers work in haulage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weathy' is a typo in the source for wealthy. The phrase once meant shoppers rich enough to keep their own carriages.
explanation.definitionFit: Carriage trade is the idiom for upmarket patrons, while carriage is also the conveying of goods for payment.

clue.text: Farewel to the Parisian about to depart

definitions.text: Farewel to the Parisian about to depart

parts.note: surface reading: saying goodbye to a person from Paris
setter's reading: the word a French speaker says on leaving

explanation.surface: Saying goodbye to a Parisian friend just before setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Farewel' is a typo in the source. The clue reads as bidding goodbye to someone, but means the word a Parisian says when leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is the French goodbye, literally 'to God', used in English too for a final parting.

clue.text: Salesman returned holding silver bleeper

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so one word encloses another
something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman comes back carrying a silver beeping gadget.
explanation.definitionFit: A pager is a small device that bleeps to alert its wearer, so it is a bleeper.

clue.text: Gets grime shifted with these kitchen devices

indicators.note: shifted means moved about, so the letters are moved into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone scrubs dirt off the gadgets in the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg timers are small sand-glasses or dials used in kitchens to time boiling eggs.

clue.text: Insect coming from Granny Smith apple, I fancy, needs help to get out

indicators.note: fancy suggests something elaborate or imagined, so the letters are reworked freely
getting something out means removing it, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
these letters are the ones removed

explanation.surface: A bug crawls out of an apple and the speaker needs help removing it.
explanation.walkthrough: Take H, E, L and P out of GRANNY SMITH APPLE I, then rearrange the thirteen letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: The praying mantis is a predatory insect named for the way it holds its forelegs as if in prayer.

clue.text: Pet one used for experimentation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small rodent kept at home
second meaning: a person or thing tested on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a lab animal, which is exactly how the two meanings meet.
explanation.definitionFit: The cavy is a popular household rodent, and its use in labs gave the idiom for any test subject.

clue.text: Staunch Conservative rightly depressed

parts.note: true means correctly, rightly
blue means sad, depressed

explanation.surface: A loyal Tory is understandably downcast.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative Party, so a true blue is a loyal Tory.
explanation.definitionFit: True blue is the idiom for an utterly loyal supporter, especially of the British Conservative Party.

clue.text: Language used by Everyman to summon dog?

parts.note: English is a language
Everyman is the setter of this crossword

explanation.surface: The puzzle's compiler calls a dog in his own tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the pen name of this puzzle's compiler, so it stands for SETTER.
explanation.definitionFit: The English setter is a gundog breed, used to find and point at game birds.

clue.text: Conduct inciting rebellion? Head of state ignored issue

indicators.note: something ignored is left out, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: sedition is speech or conduct stirring up rebellion against the state

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only that one is meant

parts.note: the first letter of state

explanation.surface: Seditious behaviour is overlooked by the leader of a country.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of SEDITION happens to be the first letter of state, so dropping it leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue of a newspaper or magazine is one edition of it.

clue.text: Hybrid fruit — tons delivered to Dundee?

indicators.note: something delivered to another is placed with it, so one piece is set next to the other

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for tons
Angelo Dundee was the famous trainer of Muhammad Ali, so Dundee hints at his first name

explanation.surface: A huge load of fruit is shipped to the Scottish city of Dundee.
explanation.walkthrough: Dundee looks like the Scottish city, but the question mark points to boxing trainer Angelo Dundee.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangelo is a cross between a tangerine and a pomelo or grapefruit, so a hybrid citrus.

clue.text: Deficiency in desert

definitions.meaning: first meaning, a noun: a fault or flaw
second meaning, a verb: to abandon one's side for another

explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' looks like a noun of sand, but it is the verb to abandon.
explanation.definitionFit: A defect is a flaw, and to defect is to abandon one's country or cause for an opposing one.

clue.text: Material brought back by head law enforcer

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: toile is a linen or cotton fabric
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: Evidence is returned by the chief of police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head law enforcer' looks like one phrase, but head belongs to the wordplay as NESS, a headland as in Loch Ness place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot Ness was the US Prohibition agent who led the Untouchables against Al Capone.

clue.text: Irish novelist reportedly having a forbidding appearance

indicators.note: reportedly means according to what is said, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: Laurence Sterne, born in Ireland, wrote Tristram Shandy

explanation.surface: An Irish author is said to look severe.
explanation.definitionFit: Stern means strict and severe in manner, so forbidding in look.

clue.text: A wild cat's light weight

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a small unit of weight

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a scrawny cat; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard, and also a small imperial unit of about 28 grams.

clue.text: Girl taking in Italian musical

indicators.note: taking something in means absorbing it inside, so one word encloses another

parts.note: Eva is a girl's name
IT is the abbreviation for Italian

explanation.surface: A young woman goes to see an Italian show.
explanation.definitionFit: Evita is the Lloyd Webber and Rice musical about Eva Perón.

clue.text: Gradually sample tea, perhaps

parts.note: a piece is a sample or portion
tea is an example of a meal; perhaps flags the example

explanation.surface: Someone slowly tastes their tea a bit at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain tea can mean the evening meal, so it is an example of a MEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Piecemeal means bit by bit, a little at a time, so gradually.

clue.text: Thomas, say, in reservoir on military machine

indicators.note: one thing on another is placed beside it, so the pieces are joined in sequence

parts.note: a tank is a reservoir for liquid
an engine of war, such as a siege engine, is a military machine

explanation.surface: A man called Thomas ends up in a reservoir on top of an army vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thomas' looks like a person, but it is Thomas the Tank Engine from the children's books and TV series.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas the Tank Engine is the most famous example of a tank engine, a locomotive carrying its water on board.

clue.text: Agreed to put on Cymbeline, ultimately

parts.note: to don is to put on clothing

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of Cymbeline

explanation.surface: A theatre company agrees to stage Shakespeare's Cymbeline in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' looks like staging a play, but it means wearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Done! is said to seal a bargain, meaning it is agreed.
